evaluation.positioning_hook: A Ph.D. candidate infiltrates a viral media cult of brain-slugged influencers to find her missing friend, only to discover the whole operation is built to weaponize attention, fear, and consent.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and commercially sticky: a young woman, a missing friend, a viral cult, and a sci-fi conspiracy that plays like a social-media nightmare. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant crowd because the satire is pointed and the world is weird, but the hook is strong enough to travel.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the interview-room opening and keeps sharpening as Jane realizes the brain-slug videos are a recruitment funnel. By the time she enters The Hub, the premise is clean: expose the people making the content and find Eve.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jane has a clear engine—smart, defensive, socially awkward, and morally stubborn—and Eve/Capp/Sterling each have distinct comic menace. The characters are vivid, though Jane carries most of the emotional weight and the supporting players are more functionally sharp than deeply layered.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a very current anxiety—algorithmic persuasion, online misogyny, influencer authenticity—and literalizes it with brain slugs in a way that feels fresh rather than generic. The fake interview format, pop-up text voices, and media-production satire give it a confident, ownable angle.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps Jane moving from campus to date to production house to hostage-style confrontation, and each reveal escalates the threat. A few stretches are more explanatory than kinetic, but the back half becomes increasingly urgent and physical.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The brain slugs are not just a gimmick; they map cleanly onto persuasion, audience capture, and ideological capture, which makes the premise feel both strange and inevitable. The final reveal that Capp is running for President gives the satire a sharp, memorable landing.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Hub, the podcast set, the fake production office, and the online-comment chorus create a specific ecosystem with its own rules and incentives. The world is story-generating, though it remains mostly concentrated around one institution rather than expanding into multiple distinct arenas.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very particular register: deadpan, anxious, satirical, and increasingly absurd without losing the threat underneath. The blend of campus comedy, internet toxicity, and sci-fi body-control gives it a hard-to-mistake tone.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the comedy and conspiracy mechanics, there’s a real thesis about consent, audience manipulation, and how people rationalize power. The script hints at a larger political and cultural machine, though it stays mostly on the surface of that system rather than fully excavating it.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jane/Eve/Capp/Sterling/Nancy/Preston/Drew create a workable ensemble engine, especially once The Hub becomes the pressure cooker. Still, the script is fundamentally driven by Jane’s POV, and several relationships function more as pressure valves than as fully generative pairings.

lead_characters.name: Jane
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, graduate student / Ph.D. candidate, bookish, socially awkward, white or unspecified.
lead_characters.hook: Jane is a dissertation-stalled academic who treats brain slugs like a moral emergency and social interaction like a hostile field study. She’s funny because she’s rigid, dangerous because she’s right, and compelling because her need to be taken seriously keeps colliding with a world that only rewards performance.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Aubrey Plaza in Ingrid Goes West or Emma Stone in Easy A: a prickly, hyper-aware lead who can play embarrassment, rage, and deadpan precision in the same scene. The role gives an actor a full comic-to-thriller arc and a final-act physical payoff.

lead_characters.name: Eve
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s, influencer / content creator, socially polished, likely white or unspecified.
lead_characters.hook: Eve is Jane’s missing friend turned glossy on-camera convert, all warm smiles, coded threats, and performative sisterhood. She’s the kind of character who can pivot from affectionate to chilling in a beat, which makes her both a betrayal and a mirror for Jane.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jodie Comer in Killing Eve or Allison Williams in Get Out a chance to weaponize charm. It lets an actor play seduction, complicity, and menace without ever leaving the smile.

lead_characters.name: Capp
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 30s, media entrepreneur / producer, polished, charismatic, controlling.
lead_characters.hook: Capp is the smooth operator who speaks in platform logic and free-market morality while quietly running coercion as a business model. He reads like a friendly fixer until the script reveals he’s the house philosophy, not just the host.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jeremy Strong in Succession or Billy Crudup in The Morning Show a chance to make manipulation feel intelligent and seductive. It’s a prestige-villain part with real monologue and power-play territory.

lead_characters.name: Sterling
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s-30s, influencer / on-camera personality, handsome, smug, performatively edgy.
lead_characters.hook: Sterling is the self-styled truth-teller who uses irony, sexual bravado, and faux-intellectual posturing to hide how easily he folds into the system. He’s comic, gross, and useful as a pressure point because he always thinks he’s winning the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Penn Badgley in You or Nicholas Braun in Succession a chance to play charisma as a trap. It’s a great part for an actor who can make arrogance funny right up until it turns predatory.

lead_characters.name: Nancy
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 30s, producer / operator, polished, strategic, media-savvy.
lead_characters.hook: Nancy is the corporate-friendly face of the machine, the one who can talk empowerment, branding, and authenticity while helping move the machinery of control. She’s less flashy than Capp, but she’s often the one translating ideology into workflow.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Sarah Snook in Succession or Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects a chance to play intelligence with a smile. It’s a sharp, scene-stealing part for an actor who can make pragmatism feel dangerous.

lead_characters.name: Kevin
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late 20s, grad student colleague, earnest, nerdy.
lead_characters.hook: Kevin starts as Jane’s mild academic foil and ends up as the story’s most surprising ally, which makes him easy to underestimate and useful when the script needs a moral pivot. He’s not flashy, but he’s the kind of character who can turn the third act by finally choosing action over passivity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jesse Plemons in Breaking Bad or Paul Dano in The Fabelmans a chance to play quiet intelligence under pressure. It offers a strong late-film turn from passive observer to active participant.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Buchanan
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Buchanan is the academic gatekeeper who talks like a mentor while normalizing the very system Jane is trying to challenge. He’s funny in a painful way, because every joke lands as a small act of dismissal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Richard Jenkins in The Visitor a chance to play authority as a mask for deeper compromise. It’s a deliciously specific supporting part for a veteran actor.

lead_characters.name: Betty
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 40s, professional friend / legal expert, grounded.
lead_characters.hook: Betty is the sane adult in Jane’s orbit, the one who can translate the absurdity into practical next steps without losing her footing. Her presence gives the script a reality check and a human cost anchor.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that gives actors like Regina Hall in support or Amy Ryan in a prestige ensemble a chance to be the audience’s sanity. It’s small but useful, with real authority in the scenes she has.

lead_characters.name: Preston
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s, meme-driven on-camera personality, edgy, immature.
lead_characters.hook: Preston is the loud, unserious chaos agent who hides behind irony and sponsorship language. He’s a useful comic irritant because he can turn cruelty into content without ever seeming to notice the difference.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave actors like Logan Lerman in a darker register or Michael Cera in a more aggressive mode a chance to play awkward entitlement. It’s a strong comic-supporting part with menace underneath.

lead_characters.name: Drew
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 40s, indie filmmaker / technical operator, world-weary.
lead_characters.hook: Drew is the behind-the-camera guy who knows exactly how fake the whole operation is and keeps working anyway. He’s a great pressure-release character because he sees the machinery clearly but has already decided to survive inside it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a character actor a dry, lived-in showcase like Richard Kind or David Paymer often gets. It’s a smart supporting part with insider texture.

lead_characters.name: Jane's Mom
lead_characters.hook: Jane’s Mom is the domestic counterweight to the chaos, equal parts nagging, oblivious, and oddly grounding. She keeps the story tethered to ordinary life even as the plot goes fully conspiratorial.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a seasoned actress a chance to play comic exasperation with real affection, like Laurie Metcalf or Margo Martindale in a supporting turn. It’s a compact but memorable mother role.

lead_characters.name: Parking Officer Jo
lead_characters.hook: Parking Officer Jo is the perfect bureaucratic absurdity: she’s technically present at the moment of crisis and completely unavailable to help. The scene works because she embodies the story’s larger joke about systems that see everything and do nothing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp cameo-style supporting role that lets an actor play deadpan authority with comic timing. It’s the kind of part that can steal a scene in under five minutes.

lead_characters.name: Desperate Greg
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 30s, nerdy grad student, socially awkward.
lead_characters.hook: Desperate Greg is the eager hanger-on who keeps trying to belong to the wrong conversation. He’s a useful comic and thematic mirror for how easily lonely people get recruited by confidence and belonging.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a classic awkward-supporting role in the vein of a Paul Rust or Martin Starr type part. It gives an actor a chance to play neediness without losing sympathy.

casting_characteristics: Lead actress needs strong deadpan/comic timing plus thriller escalation
Several roles require polished on-camera charisma
Ensemble skews 20s-60s with no child casting

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical and editorial; limited digital cleanup for phone/text overlays, video inserts, and slug POV transitions.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical slug props, squish effects, concussion beats, and a few fight/impact moments.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; contemporary genre satire with streamer-friendly adult content.

budget.note: Contemporary, interior-heavy, and largely contained to apartments, campus spaces, and The Hub; the main spend is production design for the media-house spaces and a modest practical-effects package for the slugs.

casting.note: Jane has to carry comedy, paranoia, and physical escalation, while Capp, Eve, and Sterling all need camera-ready charisma that can pivot into menace. The roles are attractive, but the lead performance lift is specific.

development.note: The satire is clear, but the script is most potent when the media-cult mechanics stay concrete and visual; the buyer conversation will focus on how broadly the brain-slug metaphor travels beyond the immediate internet-politics lane.

comp_set.title: Get Out
comp_set.why_it_comps: A socially charged genre premise that turns a seemingly familiar social setting into a controlled nightmare with a sharp satirical edge.

comp_set.title: Sorry to Bother You
comp_set.why_it_comps: The escalation from workplace/media satire into surreal body-control allegory tracks the same kind of bold tonal swing.

comp_set.title: Bodies Bodies Bodies
comp_set.why_it_comps: Young-adult social dynamics, online identity games, and a pressure-cooker ensemble all play in the same commercially legible lane.

comp_set.title: The Menu
comp_set.why_it_comps: A contained, concept-forward satire that uses a closed ecosystem to expose status, performance, and complicity.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, high-concept genre satire with a strong female lead and a sharp read on internet culture.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, slightly female-leaning, streamer-native, college-educated audience with appetite for elevated genre and cultural commentary.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, limited VFX, and a modest ensemble keep this in indie-feature territory, with spend concentrated in production design and performance.

types_of_buyers: indie distributors looking for breakout concept titles
producer-director teams in the elevated-comedy-thriller lane
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where a sharp concept, a distinctive lead, and a contained production footprint can justify a bold tonal swing. The script is built for buyers who want something topical, funny, and unsettling without requiring tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the world is specific and expandable in theory, but no separate spinoff vector is strong enough to justify franchise positioning.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which is a major advantage in a crowded indie marketplace. That clarity helps both streamer packaging and festival-to-distribution positioning.
strengths.evidence: The opening interview, the missing Eve thread, and the reveal that the brain-slug videos are recruitment content all lock the premise fast.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jane is a strong lead engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives the project a clear casting target and a performance-forward center that can sell the movie even before the concept does. It’s the kind of part that attracts actors looking for a smart, funny, high-wire turn.
strengths.evidence: Her dissertation frustration, social awkwardness, and refusal to accept the slugs’ logic drive every major turn.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The satire maps to a real cultural anxiety.
strengths.what_it_means: The brain slugs function as a clean metaphor for persuasion, audience capture, and ideological self-justification, which gives the film relevance beyond its genre wrapper. That makes it attractive to buyers who want genre with a point of view.
strengths.evidence: The Hub’s fake authenticity, the podcast staging, and the comment-chorus toxicity all reinforce the same idea.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Hub is a contained, story-generating arena.
strengths.what_it_means: A single central location with multiple content-production spaces keeps the movie producible while still feeling expansive. It also gives the film a repeatable visual grammar that can be marketed cleanly.
strengths.evidence: Podcast studio, cyclorama, editing bay, kitchen, garage, pool, and closet all live inside one media compound.

strengths.what_it_means: The movie can sell as comedy-thriller satire rather than a generic invasion story, which broadens its appeal to genre buyers looking for voice. That tonal identity is a real differentiator in the indie sci-fi space.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from awkward dating comedy to online harassment to hostage-level threat without losing its deadpan edge.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, contained, performance-forward genre satire with a clean hook and a very current target: the audience that wants internet-age paranoia with a laugh. The indie-scale footprint, strong lead role, and streamer-friendly premise make it an easy piece to imagine packaging around a sharp actress and a director with tonal control.

items.area: The satire stays broad in the middle.
items.detail: Once Jane enters The Hub, the movie spends a long stretch explaining the media ecosystem, the slug logic, and the content strategy before the plot turns fully physical. That makes the buyer conversation more conditional on tone execution than on pure page-turning momentum.

items.area: Jane carries most of the dramatic weight.
items.detail: The supporting players are vivid, but the script is structurally Jane-driven, so the movie lives or dies on one actor’s ability to hold comedy, fear, and moral certainty at once. That narrows the casting conversation more than the concept alone suggests.

The allegory is sharp for audiences tuned into social-media manipulation and ideological capture, but it is also specific enough that some buyers will ask how far the concept travels outside that lane. The movie’s appeal is real, but it is not a generic crowd-pleaser.

items.area: The final political button is provocative.
items.detail: Ending on Capp as a presidential candidate is a strong satirical sting, but it also pushes the movie into a more overtly political register than the earlier campus-and-content satire. That’s a feature for some buyers and a friction point for others.

items.area: The Not Like Us needle-drop needs clearance.
items.detail: The script specifically names "Not Like Us," which creates a real sync-clearance and budget question if the song is retained in production. It’s a manageable item, but it is a real line item rather than a placeholder.

issues.headline: The main friction is not the concept; it’s the middle stretch where the satire has to do a lot of explanatory work before the thriller engine fully takes over. Buyers will also weigh how much of the movie’s appeal depends on one lead performance and how broadly the brain-slug metaphor lands beyond the immediate internet-culture lane.
